Martes zibellina
The sable is a forest marten of northern Eurasia, widespread from the Urals through Siberia to the Pacific. It also occurs in China, Mongolia, North Korea, Kazakhstan and Hokkaido.

Adults have a long, flexible body, short feet and a bushy tail. In broad Russian samples, males measured 32–53 cm from head to body and weighed 1.15–1.85 kg; females measured 30–48 cm and weighed 0.65–1.60 kg. These observed ranges vary geographically, and adult males are usually heavier than females. Winter fur is dense and silky; the summer coat is shorter and coarser. Across populations, fur ranges from sandy brown to nearly black, sometimes with a pale throat patch. The sable resembles the European pine marten, Martes martes, but is usually darker, has a shorter tail relative to its body, and hunts more often on the ground.

The sable inhabits coniferous taiga and mixed forests on plains and mountains, hunting mainly near the ground. In Hokkaido, tracked animals rested in dense stands with fallen wood and foraged in mature forest where rodents were plentiful.

The sable is an adaptable predator, and its diet shifts with season and local prey. In eastern Hokkaido, voles occurred most often in samples, followed by Siberian chipmunks and wood mice. The same study recorded birds, eggs, insects, fish, amphibians, reptiles and crustaceans; fruits were more frequent in autumn and winter, when plant foods can supplement mammal prey. In Barguzin, sables hunt pikas beneath snow and scavenge carrion. This broad menu may help sables compensate when mammal prey fluctuates.
Sables are generally solitary, use individual ranges, locate prey by hearing and smell, and mark their surroundings with scent. In storms or during human pursuit, they may hide in dens for days.

Mating takes place mainly from mid-June to mid-August, though dates vary by region. In sparse populations, courtship may involve chasing, jumps and low rumbling; males may fight where their ranges overlap. After fertilization, the embryo remains dormant for 7.5–8 months before attaching to the uterine lining; it then develops for about 30–35 days, with births from late March to early May. Litters contain one to seven kits, often about three. Newborns are helpless and blind; they open their eyes around one month, leave the den soon afterward, and are weaned at about seven weeks, when the mother begins providing regurgitated food. Young disperse in August.

Forest structure shapes shelter and hunting: in Hokkaido, sables rested under dense cover that may reduce exposure to red foxes and wind, then foraged in rodent-rich mature stands. Some tracked home ranges overlapped extensively. Food shortages can enlarge home ranges.

Demand for sable fur drove severe depletion in parts of Russia by the early twentieth century. In 1914, a survey found only about 20–30 sables across the future Barguzin reserve; established in 1916 with a hunting ban, it enabled the population to recover. An IUCN assessment dated 3 March 2015 and published in 2016 classified the species globally as Least Concern, reflecting its large, widespread population.

Eurasian Woodcock
Scolopax rusticola

The Eurasian woodcock is a stocky, secretive wader that lives in woodland rather than on the shore. Mostly active at dusk and at night, it spends the day in dense cover, where its cryptic plumage makes it hard to see.

A plump bird 33–38 cm long, including a straight bill of 6–8 cm, with a wingspan of 55–65 cm. British adults weigh about 305 g and have a wing near 200 mm. The cryptic plumage is reddish-brown above and buff and barred below. The large eyes sit high and far back on the head, giving it very wide vision.

It is predominantly a bird of woodland, emerging at night to feed in adjacent fields. It breeds in large, unfragmented broadleaved or mixed woods with dense undergrowth, favouring birch and avoiding beech-dominated woods. Breeding needs fairly open areas, which become scarcer as conifer plantations mature.
It eats mainly earthworms, along with insects and their larvae, freshwater molluscs and some seeds. It probes soft ground with its long bill, which makes it vulnerable when the ground freezes.

Breeding males perform a display flight called roding at dusk, flying in straight lines above their territories while giving a grunting call. Most British birds are resident, but others arrive in autumn from Finland and Russia to spend the winter.

The nest is a scrape on the ground in low woodland cover. A clutch is typically 4 eggs (observed 2–5), incubated by the female for 21–24 days. The downy chicks leave the nest at once and fledge after 15–20 days. Breeding typically starts at two years of age.

The woodcock is a significant game bird in many countries. A study in Brittany found annual survival of 0.86 for adults and 0.67 for juveniles, and its authors urged caution in harvesting. Fragmentation of woodland is the main threat across its breeding range.

The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern. In the UK it is Red-listed: about 57,000 males bred in 2016 and a 2013 survey found a 29% decline since 2003, while about 1.4 million birds wintered in 2003–04. Typical life expectancy is four years, and the oldest ringed bird reached over 15 years.

Senegal galago
Galago senegalensis

The Senegal galago, also called the northern lesser galago or Senegal bushbaby, is a small strepsirrhine primate in the family Galagidae. Despite its name, it ranges far beyond Senegal across sub-Saharan Africa, from western regions toward the Horn and East Africa. Four subspecies are commonly recognised, though boundaries and some taxonomy remain under study. It is a nocturnal, tree-living primate, but regularly descends to the ground.

This galago has a compact body, soft grey to brown fur, a pale stripe down the nose, very large mobile ears, and forward-facing eyes that reflect torchlight. A reflective layer behind the retina returns some incoming light through the photoreceptors, improving the chance of detecting photons in dim conditions; it does not create light. Long fingers and toes end in broadened, grippy pads for holding branches. A comb of lower front teeth and a narrow grooming claw on the second toe of each hind foot help maintain the coat.

Across its broad range, the species uses woodland, bushland, savanna and some montane habitats rather than one uniform forest type. Local observations illustrate this flexibility: the Senegal subspecies occurs in open Acacia–baobab woodland in The Gambia, while populations elsewhere use moist woodland, riverine forest and wooded grassland. In northern Tanzania, researchers found sleeping sites with dense canopy and connected neighboring trees. Such cover can hide a resting animal from aerial predators, while connected branches provide escape routes; cooler, more humid sleeping locations also support a thermoregulatory explanation. These results describe one Tanzanian site and season, not every population.

The Senegal galago eats arthropods and tree exudates such as gum. At a northern Tanzanian site, researchers directly observed both foods but did not collect enough data to estimate their dietary proportions. During a separate dry-season study at Fongoli in southeastern Senegal, they did not see fruit eating; fruit has been recorded in The Gambia. These observations suggest local and seasonal flexibility, not one universal menu. Gum is an energy-rich plant secretion, often released after insect damage to bark, and gives the galago a food source distinct from mobile insect prey.

The galago’s night is divided between travel, feeding, pauses and self-maintenance. Powerful hind limbs and elongated ankle and foot bones help it cling upright to a trunk, then launch into a leap; elastic tendons and connective tissues store energy during crouching and release it rapidly at take-off. This spring-like mechanism amplifies muscle power, while the long tail helps stabilize the body in motion. Grooming combines licking and combing with the lower toothcomb and hind-foot grooming claw. Social life is neither strictly solitary nor continuously group-based: individuals often forage alone, but may sleep together and keep contact by calls. A Tanzanian study found social patterns differed substantially among sites.

Females bear dependent young that require milk, warmth and protection while their coordination develops. A mother may carry an infant in her mouth or let it cling to her fur, and may leave it concealed while she forages. A 1960 study of the nominate subspecies in Sudan described oestrous cycles lasting four to six weeks throughout the year, with a local peak of sexual activity in mid-December in the Nuba Mountains. This did not establish a fixed breeding season across the species. Maternal care is central; reproductive timing and male involvement remain less well documented across populations.

By eating arthropods, galagos are predators of small invertebrates, although their effect on prey populations has not been quantified well enough to claim broad ecosystem control. They also exploit gums produced when insects damage Acacia trees, linking the primate’s feeding to a plant’s response to injury and to the insects beneath the bark. A striking predator–prey interaction was documented at Fongoli, Senegal: chimpanzees sometimes probe tree cavities with sharpened sticks to capture sleeping galagos. This is a local hunting technique, not a general account of chimpanzee diets or of galago mortality across Africa.

The IUCN’s global assessment conducted in 2016 and published in 2019 classified Galago senegalensis as Least Concern, consistent with its extensive range. This category is a global risk assessment, not proof that every local population is stable or that habitat change is harmless. Nocturnal galagos are difficult to detect, and information remains sparse for many populations, making local abundance hard to establish. Woodland conversion and degradation can remove sleeping cover and feeding trees locally; the degree of risk depends on the site. The category alone does not establish the condition of any particular population.

Common Cuttlefish
Sepia officinalis

The common cuttlefish is a cephalopod mollusc of the eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean. It lives close to the seabed, hunts by ambush and can change its skin colour and texture within seconds. It breeds once and then dies, usually at about two years of age.

The mantle usually measures 30–49 cm depending on the region, with a record of 60 cm, and the body weighs 2–4 kg. An oblong internal shell, the cuttlebone, lies in the mantle. Pigment cells (chromatophores) and light-reflecting cells (leucophores and iridophores) let the skin change; the usual colour is mottled black or brown.

It lives in the eastern North Atlantic, the English Channel and the Mediterranean, with populations along West Africa as far south as South Africa. It occupies sandy or muddy bottoms from shallow water to 200 m deep, staying inshore in spring and summer and moving to 100–200 m in autumn and winter.

Crustaceans and fish form the bulk of the diet, with some gastropods, nemertean worms, polychaetes and other cuttlefish. It is an ambush predator that either shoots out its two long tentacles or pounces on prey.

Mostly nocturnal, it spends most of its time on the seafloor and buries itself in sand by day. It changes skin pattern within seconds to blend in, flees by jet propulsion through its siphon and releases ink when threatened. It is solitary except when mating.

Spawning takes place in shallow, warmer water in spring and summer; courting males display coloured bands. A female carries from 150 to 4,000 eggs, each 6–9 mm, laid in clusters on seaweed, shells and other supports. Eggs hatch in 30–90 days depending on temperature. In the English Channel the life cycle lasts two years, though a small share of males mature at one year; both sexes die after breeding.

The common cuttlefish is an active consumer with a broad, flexible niche. It is preyed on by large fish, sharks, dolphins, toothed whales and seals, and defends itself by camouflage, ink and rapid jet escapes.

The species is believed to be abundant and not threatened with extinction, but fishing is near the maximum sustainable yield. In the English Channel the stock is considered fully exploited, and in 2010–2011 animals matured at a smaller size than in the 1990s, possibly linked to fishing effort and warming seas.

Shoebill
Balaeniceps rex

The shoebill is a wetland bird and the sole living member of Balaenicipitidae. Despite its stork-like silhouette, it is neither a stork nor a heron: evidence places it closer to pelicans. Its slate-grey body, long legs, and broad, shoe-shaped bill mark this marsh hunter.

Adults are mainly blue-grey, with darker flight feathers, a pale eye, and long, widely spread toes suited to walking over floating vegetation. The enormous bill has a deep, bulbous base, sharp cutting edges, and a hooked tip; males average slightly larger.

It occupies freshwater swamps and seasonally flooded marshes across central and eastern Africa, from South Sudan south to Zambia. Dense reeds, sedges, or papyrus provide cover, while small open patches and floating plant mats offer places to fish and nest.

Fish dominate its diet, especially lungfish, bichirs, and catfish; it also takes water snakes and frogs, with other aquatic vertebrates reported less often. The bird waits motionless or walks slowly, then lunges down in a forceful forward collapse to seize prey in its bill.

Usually solitary, shoebills keep space between feeding birds, even when a pair is nesting. A successful strike may bring up fish tangled with vegetation; the bird shakes plant matter free before swallowing. It is largely sedentary, though changing water levels can prompt local movements.

Pairs nest far apart, building broad platforms of wetland vegetation on floating mats or small mounds. Clutches hold one to three eggs, commonly two; both parents incubate and tend young. Often only one chick survives, as food shortage or sibling aggression limits the brood.

The shoebill depends on a shifting mosaic: dense cover for concealment, fish-rich water, and open footing where it can recover after a lunge. In Bangweulu, Zambia, tracking found mostly short daily movements, linked to feeding and the search for suitable wetland patches.

In its profile consulted in October2026, BirdLife International lists the shoebill as Vulnerable and reports an estimate of3,300–5,300 mature individuals. These are assessment estimates, not a new census. Wetland loss, hunting, nest disturbance, illegal capture and drought are identified pressures.

Short-eared Owl
Asio flammeus

The short-eared owl is a ground-nesting owl of open country that often hunts in daylight. It is nomadic, following local booms in small-mammal numbers, and breeds in very different places from one year to the next.

It is a medium-sized owl, about 34–42 cm long with a wingspan near one metre, and it weighs around 330 g in Britain. The plumage is a mix of yellowish-white and dark brown, and it varies a good deal between individuals. Its ears sit at different heights on the sides of the head.

In Britain it breeds on upland grassland and young forestry plantations, including heather moorland, rough grassland and bogs, mainly in northern England and Scotland. In winter it uses a wider range of grasslands. Elsewhere it favours open, treeless country such as marshes.

It feeds mainly on small mammals, with the field vole especially important in Britain, and takes some birds. It hunts by flying slowly low over the ground or by pouncing from a perch, relying largely on hearing to find prey hidden in grass.

The species is nomadic rather than strictly migratory: an individual may breed in one place one year and somewhere completely different the next. Winter numbers in Britain are boosted by birds arriving from Fennoscandia. Males perform sky-dancing displays with wing-clapping, and the owls may roost communally in winter.

The nest is a scrape on the ground in tall vegetation. In Britain a clutch is typically four to seven eggs, incubated by the female for about 26 days. The chicks fledge at roughly 25–31 days, and birds typically first breed at one year old.

As a major predator of voles and mice, the owl helps control rodent populations. Its ground nests expose eggs and young to mammalian predators, and adults can fall prey to large raptors such as the northern goshawk and peregrine. It defends its nest with distraction displays such as feigning a broken wing.

The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern worldwide, but in the UK it is Amber-listed and breeding is scarce, with an estimated 620 pairs in 2007–11. Its British breeding range shrank by almost half between 1968–72 and 2008–11. The oldest ringed bird lived nearly seven years.

Siamese Fighting Fish
Betta splendens
Native to Thailand and nearby Indochina, wild B. splendens is short-finned and subdued; ornamental colours and flowing fins reflect selective breeding.
Adults average about 6.5 cm; males are often slimmer, longer-finned, and brighter, while females have shorter fins, especially in domestic strains.
It inhabits Thailand’s central plain and nearby Indochina, in shallow marshes, floodplains and rice fields with warm, slow water and vegetation.

It snaps up small animal prey among plants or at the surface, especially zooplankton and mosquito or other insect larvae. Small crustaceans and insects that fall onto the water also provide food, so access to animal prey is a central part of its natural feeding ecology.

Territorial males spread fins and flare gill covers to warn rivals; clashes can cause bites and injury. Aggression varies, and females can also be territorial. Domesticated fighting strains were selected for persistent aggression, whereas ornamental breeding later favoured elaborate fins and colours; the intensity of fighting therefore differs among strains.

The male courts beside a floating bubble nest. During an embrace, female eggs meet male sperm in water: fertilization is external. He gathers sinking eggs and guards them; after hatching, he tends larvae until they swim freely. Keeping eggs in a surface bubble nest improves their access to oxygen in warm, poorly oxygenated water, while the male repairs damaged bubbles. Incubation typically lasts about 24–36 hours, followed by two to three days in the nest while larvae absorb their yolk reserves. Young fish initially rely on their gills, because air breathing develops later; growth rate influences this transition and the age of maturity.

It eats insect larvae and feeds larger aquatic predators. A blood-rich labyrinth above the gills absorbs surface air in oxygen-poor water; gills still exchange gases underwater. The labyrinth contains folded bony surfaces lined with respiratory tissue, giving inhaled air a large exchange surface above the gills.
The IUCN’s 2011 assessment classifies wild populations as Vulnerable, citing wetland loss and pollution. Captive abundance does not secure native fish.

Snowshoe hare
Lepus americanus

This North American hare inhabits boreal and mountain forests, from Alaska and Newfoundland south to the western mountains and Appalachians. Its name recalls broad, furred hind feet that aid travel over soft snow. Herbivorous, it also feeds many mammalian and bird predators, so its abundance affects other populations. Northern numbers cycle strongly, while many southern populations fluctuate less.

Adults average 46–51 centimetres and 1.4–1.8 kilograms in Alaska; size varies regionally, so these are indicative figures. The coat usually changes from brown or grey-brown in summer to white in winter, with dark ear tips and a small tail. Large, furred hind feet spread weight over snow and reduce sinking. On coastal parts of British Columbia, Washington and Oregon, where snow is scarce, hares may remain brown year-round. Females are often slightly larger than males.

Across most of its range, the hare favors boreal or upper-montane forest with dense understory, where shrubs provide food and concealment. In California it also uses dense conifer stands, high-elevation riparian woods and chaparral. It rests in a shallow ground hollow called a form, often beneath brush, ferns or fallen timber, rather than digging a burrow. Well-used runways connect feeding patches and shelter; snow makes them conspicuous and can preserve summer routes.

In California, grasses, forbs and succulent plants are important summer foods; in snowy winters, hares there rely mainly on conifer needles and evergreen shrub leaves. Newfoundland menus include birch, willow, maple, balsam fir, grasses and fireweed, illustrating regional variation. Like other lagomorphs, hares re-ingest soft nutrient-rich droppings called cecotropes, passing food through the gut again so more nutrients can be absorbed. This helps recover nutrients from fibrous plants, while nutritious young growth remains valuable when available.

Snowshoe hares are generally solitary outside breeding, although overlapping home ranges and temporary feeding aggregations occur. They are active mainly at dusk and night, resting by day in sheltered cover. Individuals communicate partly by thumping their hind feet, a reported warning or contact signal, and may squeal when captured. Females and males may each have several mates; this does not make hares a stable social group.

Breeding dates vary with latitude and local conditions; in many northern populations, mating begins in late winter or spring and continues into summer. Gestation lasts about 36–37 days; litters range from one to six leverets and average three, with counts varying locally. A female may conceive again before her previous litter is born, allowing several litters in a long season. Leverets are born fully furred, open-eyed and mobile; they nurse once daily and become self-supporting at three to four weeks.

Lynx, coyotes and foxes hunt snowshoe hares, as do numerous hawks and owls; no single predator explains every local trend. Yukon field experiments found that reducing mammalian predation and adding food each raised hare density, while doing both had a larger combined effect. Predator numbers often follow hare abundance with a delay, and may shift to other prey when hares become scarce. At population peaks, browsing can reduce young shoots, linking plant availability with predation.

The species is widespread and classified as Secure in Canada in the 2020 General Status assessment, a national screening rather than legal protection. In California, where it occupies a limited set of high-elevation regions, the wildlife agency lists it as a Species of Special Concern. In Alaska, the wildlife agency lists development, mining and fuel exploration as habitat threats. Shorter snow seasons can leave winter-white hares conspicuous against bare ground. Montana research found mismatches during spring and autumn molts; spring color change can respond to snow conditions, but does not track every local change perfectly.

Common Sole
Solea solea

The common sole is a flatfish of the eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean that lives half buried on sandy and muddy seabeds. Its young grow up in shallow coastal nurseries, and it is a commercially valuable species for the countries around the southern North Sea.

The body is oval and strongly flattened, with both eyes on the right side of the head. The eyed side is greyish to reddish brown with large diffuse dark blotches, while the underside is white. The pectoral fin on the eyed side has a dark spot on its outer half. It reaches about 70 cm at most and is commonly 15–45 cm.

It lives in the eastern Atlantic from Norway’s Trondheim Fjord south to Senegal, in the North Sea and the western Baltic, and throughout the Mediterranean. It stays on sandy and muddy bottoms, usually at 10–60 m and down to about 150 m, and moves into deeper water in winter.
Adults feed at night on the seabed, taking mainly polychaete worms, molluscs and small crustaceans found in the sand and mud.
Adults burrow into sandy and muddy bottoms and usually live alone. After settling, juveniles move little and stay in the same nursery area, a shallow, muddy-to-sandy coastal zone.

It spawns in batches in shallow coastal water at 6–12 °C, mainly from February to May, and starts to breed at 3–5 years of age, at about 25–30 cm. In the southern North Sea, eggs hatch from early April to mid-May. The pelagic larval phase lasts about 34 days, and the young settle in nurseries between mid-May and mid-June.

In the southern North Sea, young sole depend on shallow coastal nurseries such as the Belgian coast, the Eems–Dollard estuary and the Wadden Sea, the most important nursery area. As a bottom predator, the sole feeds on worms, molluscs and small crustaceans. Its life cycle therefore ties offshore spawning to these sheltered coastal habitats.

The IUCN Red List lists the species as Data Deficient (assessed in 2014). It is commercially valuable in the southern North Sea, where there is a risk of unsustainable exploitation and large bycatch of undersized juveniles, so management focuses on reducing that bycatch.

Common Eider
Somateria mollissima

The common eider is a heavy, sociable sea duck that rarely strays far from the coast. It is the heaviest duck in the United Kingdom and a strong, fast flier; its soft nest down gave the eiderdown its name.

An adult weighs about 2.1 kg in Britain, with a wing length near 29 cm; males are slightly larger. The breeding male is white above and black below, with a black cap and a pale green patch on each side of the head. The female is brown with dense dark barring, a camouflage that hides her on the nest. Young males need about three years to reach full adult plumage.

It is a true sea duck, usually found close to shore in sandy bays or in long lines just beyond the breaking waves, and it is rarely seen on fresh water. It nests on rocky coasts and islands, often on small islands free of mammalian predators; in Britain and Ireland it breeds mainly around northern coasts and winters further south.

The eider feeds mostly on blue mussels and other molluscs, together with crustaceans and echinoderms such as crabs and sea urchins. It dives for them, in British waters typically to about 3 m, and swallows the shells whole before crushing them in its gizzard.

Eiders are very sociable, riding the swell in groups and gathering in long lines offshore. In spring the males give loud, moaning courtship calls. Ducklings leave the nest soon after hatching and often join a crèche tended by several females, which lowers the risk for each individual chick.

In the UK there is usually one brood a year, with a clutch of typically four to six eggs. The female lines the nest with her own down and incubates alone for 25–28 days. The downy chicks feed themselves and fledge after about 65–75 days. Breeding typically starts at three years of age.

By eating mussels and other shellfish, eiders shape the numbers of their prey, which has brought them into conflict with mussel farmers. Gulls are major predators of eggs and ducklings, and Arctic foxes take them where they can reach the nests, which is why islands without mammals are favoured. In Shetland, predation by marine mammals such as killer whales is one suspected factor in recent declines.

The IUCN lists the common eider as Near Threatened. The UK breeding population was about 37,000 pairs in 2012–15, and the UK wintering population fell by 32% between 1998 and 2023. It is Amber-listed in the UK, partly because of its winter concentrations, which are vulnerable to oil spills and other pollution. The oldest ringed bird reached over 35 years.

South American coati
Nasua nasua
The South American coati is a procyonid mammal of tropical and subtropical South America. Its daily life combines solitary feeding, group travel by females and young, and seasonal reproduction.

An adult measures about 41–67 cm from head to rump, with a separate 32–69 cm tail; reported mass is 3–6 kg. In a wild adult sample from three parks in Minas Gerais, Brazil, males averaged 4.36 kg and females 3.53 kg; this difference was not statistically significant. Fur ranges from grey-brown to rusty red, and the brown, flexible muzzle turns slightly upward. The ringed tail balances the animal but cannot grasp; five clawed digits and strong forelegs dig through soil and rotting wood. Mobile ankle joints let it turn its hind feet outward to climb down a trunk headfirst.

The range stretches from Colombia and Venezuela south through Ecuador and Brazil to Uruguay and northern Argentina, reaching about 2,500 m on Andean slopes. Coatis use evergreen and deciduous forests, cloud forests, riverine woods, dry scrub, Chaco, and Cerrado, with forest cover remaining central. In an urban Cerrado park in Brazil, seasonal food availability shifted coatis’ movements and daily activity.

Fruits and invertebrates are major foods, but their importance shifts with season and local availability. In Paraná, 426 scats contained frequent fruit, especially figs and Prunus brasiliensis, as well as leaves and beetles; winter samples held more invertebrates, plant matter, and vertebrate prey. It noses beneath leaf litter and claws into rotting wood for insects, larvae, ants, and termites, while also searching trees for fruit. Eggs, small vertebrates, and carrion broaden the menu when available. At Brazilian visitor sites, processed food and refuse have also appeared in coati diets.

Coatis are chiefly diurnal, foraging mostly on the ground but climbing to sleep, nest, and move through trees. Females and immature animals travel in bands, while adult males often live alone; a field study at Iguazú, Argentina, also recorded males staying with bands year-round. In a Cerrado population, seasonal food supply shifted movements and daily activity, showing that group life and space use are flexible. Members keep contact with calls and touch, groom one another, and retreat into trees or flee over ground when disturbed.

Breeding is seasonal; solitary males may temporarily join female bands to mate. Females may become receptive within a synchronized one- to two-week period; males compete, while genetic work has found some young fathered by males from outside the group. After mating, pregnant females build tree nests and raise the litter apart from the band. Gestation lasts about 74–77 days, with three to seven young; mothers reunite with the band after five or six weeks and nurse until weaning near four months. Young open their eyes at around ten days, walk at three to four weeks, and climb soon afterward; females mature near two years and males around three.

The coati consumes litter-dwelling invertebrates and is itself prey for large cats, raptors, and boas. Fruit-eating also moves seeds away from parent plants: a 33-month study in southeastern Brazil recorded fruits from 53 plant species and seeds from at least 49 in coati diets and scats. Gut passage left germination unchanged for most tested plants, but improved it for one species after pulp removal. Seed dispersal by coatis may help connect forest patches and support plant recruitment, alongside the partly overlapping services of other fruit-eating animals.

The IUCN’s global Red List assessment, published in 2016 and conducted in 2015, classified Nasua nasua as Least Concern. Its wide range and presence in protected areas support that status, though habitat loss and hunting threaten coatis locally. Near settlements, coatis may raid crops or take poultry. Studies at Brazilian visitor sites have also found human food and refuse in their diets, evidence that contact can alter foraging. Nasua nasua solitaria is listed in CITES Appendix III at Uruguay’s request.

Spring peeper
Pseudacris crucifer

The spring peeper is a tiny chorus frog native to eastern North America, from southeastern Canada through much of the eastern United States. Its shrill, repeated peep is among the first frog calls heard as spring approaches.

Adult males are often 20–30 mm long and females 30–40 mm; measurements vary among populations. Tan, brown or grey skin usually bears a dark X-shaped mark; the forefeet have four digits and the hindfeet five, tipped with adhesive pads.

It can climb but often stays near the ground, hiding in leaf litter in marshy woods or lowlands near ponds and swamps. It breeds in shallow freshwater pools, often temporary, where plants or debris can hold eggs.

Adults catch small live insects and other arthropods visually, using a sticky tongue; prey includes ants, beetles, flies and spiders. Tadpoles graze on algae and consume detritus and microorganisms in the pond.

Male spring peepers call at breeding pools at dusk and on spring evenings; the throat vocal sac is an expandable pouch that inflates and deflates during the repeated peep. In northern populations, some individuals can survive partial freezing during winter dormancy, but this tolerance is not universal.

After winter, males call at breeding sites and clasp females in amplexus, the mating hold. They externally fertilize several hundred eggs as females lay them; eggs attach singly underwater and hatch within days. Larvae usually metamorphose after roughly 45–90 days, with development partly dependent on water availability.

Spring peepers use fishless pools and also breed in temporary ponds that may dry after tadpoles transform, linking successful development to water persistence. Predators include aquatic beetle larvae for tadpoles and snakes, skunks and larger frogs for adults.

The IUCN assessed the species as Least Concern in 2020, citing its broad range, large presumed population and use of varied habitats. Wetland drainage is a minor threat globally, while intensive urbanization and agriculture can make some areas less suitable.

Arctic Tern
Sterna paradisaea

The Arctic tern is a slender seabird famous for the longest migration of any animal tracked so far. It breeds in the far north and spends the northern winter in Antarctic waters, so it enjoys two summers each year.

A small tern about 36–43 cm long with a wingspan of 74–84 cm; adults weigh around 100 g. It is white with a grey back, a black cap, long tail streamers and a deeply forked tail. In the breeding season the whole bill is red. The legs are very short, so the bird looks crouched when standing.

It breeds in high-latitude coastal areas of the Arctic and subarctic; in Britain, breeding is coastal and mainly northern. Outside the breeding season it lives mostly offshore or along coasts, and in the far south it rests on pack-ice floes. Some birds pause at lakes and reservoirs during spring migration.

It hovers above the water, then dives, often submerging completely, to catch small fish such as sand eels, sand lance and capelin, and it also takes small crustaceans. In Britain, breeding success is linked to how many sand eels are available.

Arctic terns nest in colonies and defend them vigorously. A tracking study of 11 birds fitted with tiny geolocators showed that some flew more than 80,000 km a year, using two main southbound routes along the African or South American coasts and an S-shaped route back across the Atlantic.

In the UK a clutch is typically one or two eggs, with one brood a year. Both sexes incubate for 20–24 days. The downy chicks are semi-precocial and fledge after 21–24 days. Breeding typically starts at about four years of age. Nests are shallow scrapes on sand, gravel or moss.

The tern is a predator of small fish and crustaceans, and its eggs and chicks are taken by foxes, rats, gulls and other animals. American mink are implicated in the loss of breeding range in western Scotland. In the past, DDT contamination of the fish it ate killed many terns.

The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern. In the UK it is Red-listed: the breeding population was about 54,000 pairs in 2000, and the breeding range shrank by 30.5% between 1968–72 and 2008–11. A tern that reaches breeding age typically lives about 13 years, and the oldest ringed bird exceeded 31.

Stoat
Mustela erminea

The stoat is a small mustelid with a long, slender body, short legs and a black-tipped tail. It searches covered ground and follows prey into burrows. Its coat moults seasonally, but winter whitening varies with local climate and snow conditions.

In Britain, adult males measure about 27.5–31 cm and weigh roughly 200–450 g; females are about 24–29 cm and 140–280 g. Tails measure 9.5–14 cm in both sexes. In summer the back is chestnut to reddish brown and the underside pale; the black tail tip remains in winter. The smaller least weasel, Mustela nivalis, lacks this black tip. Stoats moult twice yearly: day length helps set the seasonal timing, while temperature affects whether winter fur becomes fully white or stays mottled. A study of Dutch pelts found full winter whiteness more often in colder regions. When snow disappears, a white coat can stand out against bare ground.

Stoats occupy a broad range of covered habitats, from grassland and farmland to woodland, marsh and upland; in Britain they travel along hedgerows, ditches and stone walls. A 2021 genetic and morphometric revision assigns M. erminea mainly to the Old World and Beringia into Alaska; most continental North American populations are M. richardsonii, while Haida Gwaii and Alexander Archipelago island populations are M. haidarum.

Small mammals, especially rabbits and water voles where abundant, are staple prey; stoats also take rodents, birds and eggs. A British stomach-content study found lagomorphs most often, followed by rodents and birds or eggs; in that sample, males ate more lagomorphs and females more small rodents. Stoats enter wider prey tunnels, such as rabbit, rat and water-vole burrows, and climb to reach birds’ nests. Most prey are killed with a bite to the back of the neck. Stoats cache surplus prey and reuse former prey nests as dens, sometimes lining them with fur in cold regions.

Stoats are mostly solitary: adult males and females occupy separate territories, and males range more widely when searching for mates. Scent marks communicate territorial presence and social status. At about eight weeks, kits begin hunting alongside their mother.

In wild stoats in New Zealand, females mate in September–November and give birth the following September–October. The fertilised egg remains dormant in the uterus for about eight to nine months before implantation. After implantation, active pregnancy lasts about four weeks. Spring litters usually contain six to twelve young, born blind, deaf and sparsely furred. Mothers care for the kits until they become self-sufficient at around twelve weeks. Female kits can mate at only two or three weeks old, before leaving the nest.

In Britain, stoat abundance often tracks prey populations, especially rabbits; myxomatosis-driven rabbit crashes coincided with sharp stoat declines in the 1950s and 1960s. A recent climate projection for the Italian Alps suggests its local range may contract as snow cover declines and snow voles shift distribution, but this is a regional forecast rather than a measured global trend. On Orkney, introduced stoats prey on endemic voles and ground-nesting birds, and compete with native raptors for voles. New Zealand stoats were introduced from Britain in the nineteenth century to control rabbits, but they have had a devastating effect on native birdlife.

England’s 2021 mammal assessment classed the stoat as Least Concern but also described its population evidence as highly data deficient. In Britain, hedgerow loss and rabbit declines may reduce habitat or food. On Orkney, where they were first recorded in 2010, an eradication programme targets this introduced predator to protect native wildlife.

Tawny owl
Strix aluco

The tawny owl is a stocky, resident woodland owl of much of Europe and parts of Asia and North Africa. It hunts mainly at night, often from a perch, and stays close to a familiar territory through the year. A rounded head without ear tufts, dark eyes and richly patterned brown or grey plumage make it recognizable even when its bark-like colours conceal it against a tree. The North African form mauritanica, sometimes separated as the Maghreb owl, is included within Strix aluco by the 2025 Clements checklist.

Adults have a rounded head, a plain facial disc, a short hooked bill and no raised ear tufts. The eyes are dark brown to nearly black and face forward. Across Europe, plumage ranges from chestnut red-brown through grey-brown to paler grey; these are colour forms within the species, not separate sexes. Males and females look alike, although females are larger on average and the size ranges overlap. Fine streaks and mottling break up the outline against bark. The broad, rounded wings and compact body suit manoeuvring among trees.

Broad-leaved and mixed woodland provide mature trees, sheltered roosts and cavities for nesting. Tawny owls also occupy conifer plantations, wooded parks and large gardens, provided that trees or nest boxes offer a suitable cavity and nearby ground supplies prey. They avoid extensive open country and uplands without tree cover. Adults remain on established territories year-round; young birds usually disperse only a few kilometres, and large stretches of water can impede their spread. Habitat quality therefore depends on both nesting sites and connected, huntable cover.

Small mammals, especially mice and voles, are common prey, but the owl takes whatever suitable animals are available: small birds, amphibians, large insects and earthworms. On damp nights it may catch worms on lawns; observations also include bats near roosts. Pellet studies show why a single menu cannot describe every pair: prey remains vary with season, habitat and local animal abundance, and the owls can switch to other prey when rodents are scarce. Fur, feathers and bones that cannot be digested are regurgitated as compact pellets, which let researchers reconstruct local feeding patterns.

This is a mainly nocturnal hunter that often waits on a perch, watches for movement, then glides down to seize prey with its feet. Its broad facial disc helps collect sound, while forward-facing eyes provide overlapping vision for judging distance. Tawny owls can locate prey by listening as well as looking. Their flight is very quiet, though not literally soundless: experiments on tawny owl wings found that removing leading-edge feather serrations increased noise shortly before landing, showing that the effect depends on flight phase. A male’s territorial hoot and a female’s sharper “keewik” may overlap as a pair duet. The familiar “twit-twoo” is therefore often two birds’ calls, not one individual producing a single phrase.

Pairs nest in tree cavities or nest boxes and may lay their first eggs as early as February in Britain, although many begin in March or later. Incubation starts with the first egg, so chicks hatch at different times; when food is limited, this can allow at least some of the brood to survive. Young leave the nest while still unable to fly. During this “branching” stage they climb, hop and flutter around nearby branches, calling to adults, which continue to find and feed them outside the cavity. Leaving the nest is thus a normal developmental step, not proof that a chick has been abandoned.

By feeding on small mammals and changing prey when their numbers fluctuate, tawny owls link woodland food webs to local prey communities. Pellet contents offer a practical record of that relationship: a two-territory study in Ukraine found seasonal, annual and habitat variation in mammal remains, with alternative prey represented as well as rodents. The owl’s dependence on cavities also ties its breeding distribution to the supply of old trees and nest boxes. Because established pairs defend territories through the year, suitable nesting cavities and hunting ground must occur within the same local landscape.

BirdLife International’s global owl-species account consulted on 11 October 2026 lists the tawny owl as Least Concern. That global category does not mean every national population is secure: in Britain, the British Trust for Ornithology reports that the species has been Amber-listed since 2015 because of concern about long-term decline. British monitoring remains incomplete because a nocturnal bird is difficult to survey, and the BTO identifies population change, breeding success and survival as continuing knowledge gaps. Availability of nest cavities and prey also shapes local suitability, so national concern and global category describe different geographic scales.

Common starling
Sturnus vulgaris

The Common Starling is a medium-sized, adaptable songbird native across much of Europe and temperate Asia. It moves between open feeding grounds and sheltered roosts, and often nests in cavities in trees or buildings. Its seasonal plumage, varied calls and large coordinated flocks make it conspicuous, while its ecological effects depend strongly on whether it lives within or beyond its native range.

Adults have a compact, dark body, short tail, pointed wings and a slender bill. The apparent blackness is broken by green, blue and purple iridescence: ordered melanosomes beneath a thin keratin layer in feather barbules produce structural colour whose hue changes with illumination and viewing angle. After the annual moult, fresh feathers carry pale tips that create conspicuous winter spots; abrasion gradually removes the tips towards spring, exposing the darker glossy feather. The bill is dark in winter and becomes yellow as breeding approaches. In breeding condition, the lower bill base is usually blue-grey in males and pink in females. A late-winter bird can therefore show both residual white spots and a yellow bill.

Starlings use open country with short vegetation, including pasture, lawns, parks and cultivated fields, where the ground is accessible for probing. Trees, reedbeds and buildings provide night roosts; nest sites are cavities such as old woodpecker holes, tree hollows, nest boxes and gaps in structures. Their broad use of human-shaped landscapes helps explain successful establishment in several introduced regions, but does not make every introduced population equally damaging.

The diet shifts with season and opportunity. During much of the breeding season, adults search soil for invertebrates such as beetle larvae and other prey, which also provide protein for growing chicks; in other periods they take fruit, seeds and other available foods. A characteristic feeding sequence is to insert the closed bill into turf or soft soil, then force it open to widen the gap and expose hidden prey. This probing-and-gaping action reaches food beneath the surface, unlike simple picking from foliage.

They forage in loose groups and gather in larger flocks at communal roosts, especially outside the breeding season. Before settling, flocks may wheel in dense aerial displays called murmurations. Measurements and models of starling flocks show that birds adjust direction and speed in response to nearby flockmates; local reactions can spread through the group, so no central leader is needed. Rapid turns propagate as birds respond to nearby flockmates and predators. Starlings also produce whistles, rattles and imitations within their vocal repertoire.

Starlings nest in cavities, where the male begins a nest of grasses and other material and the female helps finish it. A clutch usually contains three to six eggs; both parents incubate, and both feed the helpless hatchlings. Chicks remain in the nest for roughly three weeks before fledging, then continue to depend on adults while learning to forage. Some populations can raise a second brood when conditions allow. Nest cavities are a limiting resource in many landscapes, so competition for them can be intense.

Within its native range, the starling consumes soil invertebrates and fruit and also supplies prey to predators. Its probing can affect the availability of pasture invertebrates, while large feeding flocks may concentrate pressure on particular fields. In North America, where it was introduced, competition for nest cavities can displace native cavity-nesting birds; a 2003 analysis of 27 native North American cavity-nesting species detected few population declines potentially attributable to starlings. The balance of effects is therefore local and evidence-dependent, rather than a universal property of the species.

Global assessments classify the Common Starling as Least Concern because of its very large range and population. That category masks substantial regional differences. In the UK, the species is Red-listed: the British Trust for Ornithology reports a 61% decline in the breeding population from 1995 to 2024, and links concern to losses in pastoral farmland and reduced access to food. In North America and parts of Australasia it is introduced and can compete for nest cavities or cause agricultural problems, leading to local control policies. Conservation status and management therefore need a stated geography; a global category does not describe the condition of every regional population.

Appalachian Cottontail
Sylvilagus obscurus

The Appalachian cottontail is a secretive rabbit of the Appalachian Mountains of eastern North America, living in dense shrubby and coniferous cover at higher elevations. It was described as a species only in 1992 and is very similar to the eastern cottontail.

A medium-sized cottontail about 39–43 cm long, weighing roughly 0.7 to 1.5 kg depending on the source. The back is yellowish to reddish brown mixed with black, the belly whitish, and the tail fluffy and white beneath. The short, rounded ears have black front edges, and there is a small black spot between the ears but no white forehead patch; reliable identification may need skull features.

It lives in dense cover of mountain laurel, rhododendron, blueberry and conifers such as red spruce, mostly above about 760 m, though it is reported lower in Tennessee and Alabama. It also uses young clearcuts and reclaimed mining land. Its range runs from northern Pennsylvania and the Hudson River area south to northern Alabama and Georgia.

In summer it eats grasses, clover and other herbs, shrubs, buds, seeds and fruit, and in winter it shifts toward woody plant material. Like other rabbits, it eats its own droppings to recover nutrients.

It rests under dense vegetation or logs by day and forages near cover after sunset, rarely entering open areas. Radio-tracking at Dolly Sods, West Virginia, gave summer home ranges of about 6–13 ha and winter ranges of about 1.5–9 ha, with winter use concentrated in evergreen cover. It escapes predators by leaping and zigzagging.

The breeding season runs roughly from late winter to late summer. Females have several litters a year of three to eight young after a gestation of about 28 days, and only females care for the young in a shallow nest of fur and grass covered with leaves. Young leave the nest at about two weeks and are nearly independent after about a month.
It is prey for owls, hawks, foxes and dogs, and it spreads seeds by eating fruit. In areas heavily disturbed by people, it appears to be displaced by the eastern cottontail.

The Mammal Diversity Database lists it as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List. In Alabama it is poorly known and of high conservation concern, hunting does not seem to threaten it, but habitat fragmentation and development do. Its need for extensive unbroken forest and displacement by the eastern cottontail are the main limits noted in Virginia.

Little Grebe
Tachybaptus ruficollis
The little grebe is the smallest of the grebes in Britain: a shy, dumpy diving bird of ponds and lakes. It is often hidden among vegetation and betrays itself by its high-pitched, whinnying trill.

A small, dumpy grebe whose rear often looks fluffy, with an adult weight of about 225 g and a wing length near 104 mm; one account gives a body length of about 29 cm. In summer it has a bright chestnut throat and cheeks and a pale gape patch at the base of the bill.
In Britain and Ireland it breeds most often on lakes and ponds, including small farm ponds and urban parks. In winter it also uses rivers, streams and some brackish and coastal sites.
A field guide from Kenya describes a diet of insects and their larvae, small fish, frogs and tadpoles, small crustaceans and molluscs, all caught by diving.

It dives readily when disturbed and surfaces unseen some way off, rather than flying. Its feet are set far back on the body, so it is awkward on land. Birds that breed in Britain make short moves to wintering sites, and others arrive from elsewhere.

The nest is a floating platform of vegetation anchored to submerged plants. There are typically two broods, each of four to six eggs, incubated by both sexes for 20–21 days. The downy chicks leave the nest quickly and sometimes ride on a parent’s back; they fledge after about 44–48 days. Breeding typically starts at one year.

In Britain, nests succeed more often on ponds and lakes than on rivers and streams, where fluctuating water levels cause flooding failures. In Africa, tawny eagles, herons and Cape clawless otters are among its predators. The oldest ringed bird in Britain lived just over six years.

The IUCN Red List classes it as Least Concern. The UK breeding population was about 5,500 pairs in 2016, with some 16,000 birds in winter. It is Green-listed in the UK, after a spell on the Amber list during a decline in 2009–15, and has been broadly stable in Europe since 1990.

Mauritian Tomb Bat

The Mauritian tomb bat is an insect-eating bat of Africa south of the Sahara and of several Indian Ocean islands. It is named after the island of Mauritius, where the first specimen was collected, and is listed as Least Concern.

A small bat with a forearm of 60–66 mm and a weight of about 20–36 g. The back fur is short, sleek and mixed grey and the underside is entirely white. The wings are long, narrow and pale, with shortened tips that help the bat crawl when the wings are folded. Males have a dark spot on the chin.

It prefers moist, open country and savanna receiving at least about 500 mm of rain a year; in drier areas it is recorded near swamps and rivers. It also occurs in forest and along watercourses. The Mammal Diversity Database gives its range as South Africa to Sudan and Somalia and to Senegal, plus Madagascar and islands such as Mauritius, Réunion and Aldabra.

It feeds on flying insects, with moths as the staple and termites and butterflies as additions. It starts hunting once it is fully dark, spots prey over open ground and never flies above treetop height. It makes dives of up to 10 m, calling faster as it dives, and sometimes darts out of its roost by day to catch passing prey.

It roosts in the open but out of direct sun, on the outside of walls under eaves or on large tree trunks and palm trunks, choosing spots that allow a clear take-off; it does not use dark hollows or roofs as many bats do. Colonies are small, usually about five and at most about thirty. Roosts are reused year after year. Seasonal movements are suspected but not proven.

A single young is born at a time, and the female raises it alone, the young clinging to her belly until it can fly. Gestation is about two months. The timing is not settled: one source gives two birth periods a year, November–December and February–April, while another gives different months.
By eating large numbers of insects it helps control pests. Snakes and owls prey on it. It can carry parasites of the genus Anchitrema, which may pass between bats sharing the same roost.

It is listed as Least Concern, as it is widespread across Africa and nearby islands. The sources read name no specific threat. As it depends on exposed roost sites, the loss of suitable walls and trees could matter locally, but this has not been measured.

Arctic Grayling
Thymallus arcticus

The Arctic grayling is a cold-water freshwater fish of northern North America and Siberia, known for a huge sail-like dorsal fin. Among salmonids it needs some of the coldest water, and it makes long seasonal migrations between wintering, spawning and feeding areas.

The dorsal fin is greatly enlarged, with 17–25 rays, especially in males. The back is dark purple to blue-black, the sides grey to dark blue with pinkish iridescence, and the belly grey to white, with scattered dark spots. The mouth is small. Common length is about 34 cm, and the maximum is about 76 cm and 3.8 kg.

Adults live in the open water of clear, cold, medium to large rivers and lakes, from Hudson Bay to Alaska and south into Canada and the upper Missouri River in Montana; in Eurasia it occurs from the Ob to the Yenisei. Temperatures above 15 °C are stressful, and above 20 °C they cannot be tolerated for long. A population in Michigan has disappeared.
Young fish feed on zooplankton and gradually switch to immature insects. Adults feed mainly on insects at the surface, but also eat fishes, fish eggs, planktonic crustaceans and lemmings.

Each year it moves between overwintering sites, spawning streams and summer feeding areas, sometimes covering well over 100 miles. In autumn it leaves many small tributaries before they freeze or dry. Adults hold in swifter water, and larger fish tend to stay in the cooler upper reaches of a river.

Spawning takes place in spring, around ice breakup, over shallow riffles of small gravel. The fish build no nest; vibrations of the spawning pair’s tails leave a slight depression. A female lays 1,500–30,000 eggs of about 2.5 mm, which hatch in about two and a half weeks, and fish mature at roughly three to four years. Males defend a spawning area for up to a week and display their fins to females.
Its summer distribution is shaped by water temperature and by competitors such as rainbow trout. It is preyed on by pike, trout, bald eagles, ospreys, river otters and mink.

The IUCN lists it as Least Concern (assessed 2008, as reported by FishBase). In Alaska it is abundant and widespread, though populations near Nome are considered vulnerable, and slow turnover on the Seward Peninsula leaves small populations slow to recover. Mining, roads, dewatering and sedimentation are the main habitat concerns, and North American populations have been described as declining.

Tiger
Panthera tigris
The tiger is Asia’s largest wild cat, surviving in populations from the Russian Far East through South and Southeast Asia to Sumatra.

Its orange coat carries dark vertical stripes, a pale underside and conspicuous white marks behind the ears. The pattern is individual, so researchers can identify tigers in repeated photographs. Across populations, reported adult head-and-body lengths span about 150–230 cm, with tail length reported separately at 90–110 cm, and masses 75–325 kg; this broad interval is not one average or a record size. Males are larger than females, and large continental animals are not representative of every population. A broad skull, long canines and powerful jaw and forelimb muscles help seize and control heavy prey.

Tigers occur in tropical rainforests and mangroves, dry forests and scrub, grasslands, and temperate forests with heavy snow. This breadth reflects ecological flexibility, but climate alone does not make a site suitable: adequate cover, water and large wild prey are essential, and prey availability influences how much space a tiger needs.

Deer and wild pigs make up much of the diet; gaur, banteng and buffalo are important prey in some regions. Tigers also take smaller mammals, birds, reptiles and fish. Livestock may be taken where people and tiger habitat overlap. A semi-arid forest study at Ranthambhore, India, found that sambar and chital supplied most recorded prey biomass, while livestock still contributed a smaller share. That local result shows why prey choice and reliance on domestic animals should not be generalized across the range. The tiger usually stalks under cover and attacks at close range instead of pursuing prey far. Its weight and forelimbs knock an animal down; a nape bite can damage the spinal cord of small prey, while a throat bite can suffocate larger prey. After a kill, the tiger may drag the carcass into cover, tear off meat with its carnassial teeth and return to feed over several days.

Adults generally live alone. Males tend to occupy larger ranges that overlap several females; in one Thai population, neighboring females’ ranges overlapped little, while males’ ranges covered most of the female ranges they overlapped. Female home ranges tend to be smaller where prey is more abundant, though their exact area varies by landscape. Scent marks, ground scrapes, claw marks and calls let tigers exchange information without frequent direct encounters; roars, grunts and softer contact sounds serve different social purposes. Their muscular forelimbs support movement on land and help control prey. They swim well and have even been recorded hunting in water.

Breeding can occur in any season. After several receptive days, gestation lasts about 100 days and usually produces two or three cubs, though litter size varies. Newborns are blind and helpless; their mother nurses them in a den and protects them alone. Cubs begin following their mother at about two months; weaning generally occurs between three and six months. They join hunting trips at five or six months. Young gradually become independent; in a Chitwan field study, they left their natal ranges at 19–28 months. In Ranthambhore, males dispersed later on average than females. Females mature around three to four years and males around four to five.

Prey-rich areas can support denser tiger populations and smaller female home ranges than landscapes where ungulates are scarce, linking tiger distribution to the prey base. Predation can shape herbivore communities, but wider effects depend on local food webs. A field experiment in northeastern China found that birds including crows, jays and woodpeckers used simulated remains of Amur tiger prey, showing how kills can also provide carrion to scavengers.

The IUCN assessed the tiger on 15 December 2021 and published its Red List account in 2022, classifying the species as Endangered. The estimate was 3,726–5,578 wild individuals, excluding cubs, with 3,140 mature individuals as the best estimate. It combines national data collected in different years and with different methods, so it is not a synchronized census and its higher value than older editions alone does not prove growth. The assessment reports that occupied range contracted by more than half over three generations. Poaching for illegal trade, hunting of prey, habitat conversion and fragmentation remain major pressures; prey depletion and conflict with people also cause local losses and retaliatory killing.

Tench
Tinca tinca

The tench is a thickset freshwater fish of the carp family that lives in still, weedy waters across most of Europe and western Asia. It is a slow, bottom-dwelling species, tolerant of poor oxygen, and has been introduced to many other regions.

A medium-sized, thickset fish with a large head, a blunt snout, small orange-red eyes and one small barbel at each corner of the mouth. The fins are thick and rounded, the scales very small and covered in heavy mucus. The colour ranges from dark olive to golden. Mature males have larger pelvic fins, whose second ray is thickened. The common length is about 20 cm, and the maximum is about 70 cm and 7.5 kg.

It prefers still or slow water with a muddy bottom and abundant plants, typically shallow, densely vegetated lakes and backwaters, and avoids fast current. It is native to most of Europe, apart from Ireland, northern Scandinavia and parts of the Balkans, and eastward to western Siberia. Adults tolerate low oxygen and often spend the winter buried in mud.

Adults feed on the bottom, mainly on molluscs, other benthic animals and plant material, together with detritus. Elsewhere they are described as eating aquatic insects and small crustaceans, and the young take smaller prey such as microcrustaceans and midge larvae.

The tench is nocturnal and finds food more by taste and smell than by sight, which helps it in murky water. It is slow-growing and long-lived, and may reach 20 years or more, although longevity figures in the sources come from introduced populations.

Males mature at 2–3 years and females at 3–7 years. Spawning takes place from May to September, in dense vegetation at about 19–20 °C. Females lay sticky eggs in several batches over roughly two months, and the eggs hatch in a few days. The larvae stay attached to plants for several days.

As a bottom feeder of weedy shallows, the tench eats molluscs and other benthic animals and depends on vegetation for spawning. Introduced outside Europe, for example to Tasmania in 1876, it has become established in places; in Australia’s Murray–Darling Basin it is now declining and rare.
The tench is Least Concern on the IUCN Red List (assessed in 2022). It is widespread and often introduced, so it is not considered at risk across its range.

White-lipped Island Pit Viper
Trimeresurus insularis

The white-lipped island pit viper is a venomous, fully tree-dwelling snake of Java and the Lesser Sunda Islands of Indonesia, and of Timor-Leste. It is related to the white-lipped pit viper of mainland Southeast Asia and is known for its colour forms, including a rare blue one.

There are three fairly distinct colour forms: green, found across the Lesser Sundas, blue, reported only on Komodo and Padar, and yellow, on Flores. The tail tip carries a conspicuous red stripe along its upper surface. The sources read give no body length, so none is stated.

It occurs on Bali, Java, Flores, Lombok, Sumba, Sumbawa, Timor, Komodo and other islands, and in Timor-Leste, with the type locality at Soe on Timor. It generally stays in bushland and bamboo forest but sometimes enters inhabited areas in search of food.

It eats mice and lizards. A field naturalist suggested that skinks of the genus Sphenomorphus, very common on the islands he visited, probably make up much of its diet, but this is an inference, not a measurement.

It is a fully arboreal snake, though one was seen crossing the forest floor at night on Komodo. It uses caudal luring, raising and wriggling its tail like a worm to attract prey. It is described as an aggressive predator that tends to stand its ground rather than flee.

The Reptile Database lists the species as ovoviviparous, meaning the eggs develop inside the female and she gives birth to live young. A field account notes that different colour forms can appear in the same litter. Litter size and breeding season were not found.

As a predator of small lizards and rodents in island scrub and forest, it takes its place in local food webs. Its tail lure is the only hunting tactic described in the sources read. Its colour forms differ in abundance between islands for reasons that remain unclear.

The Reptile Database lists it as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. It is one of the most common causes of venomous snakebite on Bali, according to a magazine article citing an Australian Museum herpetologist; its haemorrhagic venom rarely kills but can cause severe swelling, tissue damage and bleeding. Its taxonomy is not settled across authors.

Eurasian Wren
Troglodytes troglodytes

The Eurasian wren is a tiny, round songbird and one of the most numerous breeding birds in Britain. It is often heard before it is seen: a male defends his territory with a song far louder than his body size suggests.

An adult weighs about 10 g and has a wing length near 49 mm. The plumage is brown with dark barring on the wings, tail and underparts, a pale stripe above the eye and a paler throat. The short tail is often held upright. The sexes look alike; juveniles are darker.

In Britain it is most frequent in deciduous woodland, but it also lives in scrub, pastoral farmland, villages, towns and conifer woods. It favours dense vegetation close to the ground, where it forages and finds nest sites.
The wren forages mostly on the ground, picking up insects and their larvae, spiders and millipedes. Beside water it may also take aquatic invertebrates.

Males use song to establish and defend territories, often singing from low perches. A male also builds several domed nests of moss, grass and twigs, frequently in holes; these are known as cock nests.

In Britain, laying begins on average in early May. A clutch is typically five or six eggs, incubated by the female for 16–18 days. The chicks are downy and helpless, and fledge after roughly 14.5–18 days. The female usually raises the brood. Breeding typically starts at one year of age.

Wrens help regulate insect populations and are themselves prey for domestic cats and for birds such as jays and magpies; crows and jays also raid nests. The common cuckoo sometimes parasitises wren nests.

The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern. The UK breeding population was estimated at 11 million territories in 2016 and has risen by 127% since 1967, though numbers fall after severe winters and then recover. A wren typically lives about two years; the oldest recorded in Britain reached over seven.

Tufted Duck
Aythya fuligula
The tufted duck is a compact diving duck of lakes and ponds, named for the drooping crest on the back of its head. It is common across much of Britain, including on park lakes in towns and cities.

In Britain adults weigh about 850 g, males slightly more than females, with a wing near 205 mm. The male is black with white flanks and a bright yellow eye; the female is brown with a white belly and also has yellow eyes. Both have a crest, longer and blacker in the male, and white under the wing.

In the breeding season it favours lakes, with ponds also common, and nests in dense vegetation near the water. In winter it spreads across much of Britain on lakes and ponds, including in towns and cities. It prefers shallow lakes with dense reeds for breeding.

It dives to feed on aquatic invertebrates and bivalve molluscs, with mussels such as the zebra mussel an important food. It also eats some plant matter. Ducklings eat insects from the water surface at first.

The tufted duck is highly aquatic and is often seen diving, sometimes springing slightly out of the water to start a dive. Birds are social outside the breeding season, while males defend territories around nests in spring. Courtship includes bill-dipping and neck stretches, and winter numbers in Britain are boosted by visitors from as far as central Russia.

In Britain a clutch is typically eight to eleven eggs, incubated by the female for about 25 days. The downy chicks feed themselves soon after hatching and fledge at roughly 45–50 days. Only the female provides direct care, and birds typically first breed at one year old.

As a diver on mussels and other invertebrates, the tufted duck can strongly affect those prey populations. Eggs and young fall prey to crows and mammals, and adults to foxes and large birds of prey; incubating females rely on camouflage. It also hosts a parasite that uses molluscs as an intermediate host.

The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern worldwide, but it is considered Near Threatened in Europe, and Green-listed in the UK. Britain holds about 17,000 breeding pairs (2016) and about 140,000 wintering birds, though the winter count fell 21% between 1998 and 2023. The oldest ringed bird lived over 24 years.

Song Thrush
Turdus philomelos
The song thrush is a medium-sized thrush known for its loud, musical song, often delivered at first light and at dusk. It is also famous for smashing snails on a stone to get at the soft body inside.

About 20–23.5 cm long, smaller and browner than a mistle thrush, and smaller than a blackbird. British adults weigh about 75 g and have a wing near 119 mm. The upperparts are warm brown and the creamy breast is speckled with small, upside-down heart-shaped spots.

In Britain it is most frequent in deciduous woodland, and is also common in scrub, villages and conifer woods. It has adapted to using parks and gardens for feeding and breeding. In winter it may join mixed thrush flocks in fields and orchards.

It is omnivorous, eating mainly snails and earthworms, plus soft fruit and berries. It breaks snail shells against a favourite stone, called an anvil; broken shells beside a stone or wall reveal its presence. Nestlings are fed mostly worms, slugs and insect larvae.

The song is made of short phrases, each repeated two or three times, which earned it the old name “thricecock”. It sings at dawn and as darkness falls. The species is a partial migrant: some northern European birds winter in Britain and Ireland, others go farther south.

The female builds a cup nest lined with mud and dry grass, usually in a bush or tree, and lays typically 4 glossy blue eggs lightly spotted with black or purple. She incubates for about 14 days; the chicks fledge after about 14 days. Two or three broods a year are normal. Breeding typically starts at one year.

Adults are taken by cats, little owls and sparrowhawks; magpies, jays and grey squirrels raid eggs and nestlings. Earthworm availability, which depends on soil conditions such as field drainage, affects how well thrushes can feed.

The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern, and Europe holds an estimated 40–71 million birds. In the UK, about 1.3 million territories were estimated in 2016, but numbers fell by 45% between 1967 and 2024 and the species is Amber-listed. Suspected causes include loss of hedgerows and changes in farming.

Common Guillemot
Uria aalge

The common guillemot is a diving seabird that comes to land only to breed. It nests shoulder to shoulder in dense colonies on sea cliffs, some holding tens of thousands of birds, and spends the rest of its life at sea.

A breeding adult is about 38–43 cm long, with a dark brown head, neck and back and white underparts. In winter the cheeks and throat turn white. It is less black than the razorbill, and a “bridled” form has a white ring around the eye and a white line behind it. British adults weigh about 770–1010 g.

It breeds on steep rocky cliffs, offshore stacks and islands. On mainland cliffs, pairs use narrow ledges that predators cannot reach, and on predator-free islands they nest among rocks or on bare ground. Outside the breeding season it lives in coastal waters, most abundantly in the northern North Sea and off western shores.

Sandeels are a key prey in Britain, and the diet also includes herring, capelin, marine worms, amphipods, shrimp, molluscs and squid. It dives for its food, usually to about 30 m, and can stay under for up to a minute.

It uses its strong wings to “fly” underwater. It flies strongly in the air but has to run across the water to take off. Severe winter storms can stop it from feeding and cause starvation; large seabird wrecks occurred on British coasts in the winter of 2013–14.

A pair lays a single pear-shaped egg on bare rock, once a year. Both parents incubate it for 28–37 days. The downy chick leaves the ledge after only 18–25 days, jumping to the sea and following the male, and can fly at about 39–46 days. Breeding typically begins at five years old.

Crows and herring gulls take eggs and chicks, especially in small colonies that give less protection. Changing sea temperatures are altering the abundance and distribution of sandeels, which may force the birds onto less nourishing prey and lower breeding success. Spending its life on the water makes the species vulnerable to oil spills.

The IUCN global category is Least Concern, and the species is Amber-listed in the UK. The UK breeding population was 950,000 pairs in 1998–2002; the later Seabirds Count census found about 8% fewer birds, with falls in the north and rises in the south. A bird that reaches breeding age lives about 23 years; the oldest ringed bird passed 40.

Eurasian water vole
Arvicola amphibius

The Eurasian water vole, Arvicola amphibius, is a wetland rodent widespread across Europe and northern Asia. Its range reaches from Britain east through Russia to Siberia, and south into the Middle East. Most populations live beside water, while some use damp grasslands and other less aquatic habitats. The IUCN classified it as globally Least Concern in 2023, despite regional declines.

Adults are usually 14–22 cm long, with a 9.5–14 cm tail, and weigh 150–300 g. A blunt muzzle, fur-hidden ears and furry tail distinguish it from the brown rat, which has a pointed face and bare tail. The coat is usually chestnut or dark brown above, greyish below; some populations are entirely black. Continuously growing incisors cut vegetation, and broad molars grind it.

The waterside form favours slow streams, ditches, ponds, marshes and reedbeds with soft banks and dense cover. It stays near water but travels and feeds mostly on land, often under grass. Bank burrows contain nest chambers and may open both above and below water, offering escape from danger. Some northern and upland populations also occupy wet grassland or moorland away from rivers.

It is chiefly herbivorous and may eat plant matter approaching 80 percent of its body mass daily. Grasses, sedges, rushes and waterside herbs dominate, supplemented by roots, bulbs, shoots and fruit. It carries cut stems to feeding spots and stores vegetation underground for lean periods. Pregnant females sometimes seek protein-rich snails or flowers. In captive water voles, the caecum, a pouch in the large intestine, enlarged on cellulose-rich food; pellet-eating (coprophagy) also became more frequent.

It swims and dives over short distances but is no aquatic specialist: it breathes air with lungs, and its coat can become waterlogged. A compact body and burrows help it escape predators; most feeding and resting occur on land. Activity peaks by day and at twilight, varying with season. Along streams, females often defend breeding territories while males range farther and overlap several females; studies in other habitats find looser boundaries. Scent marks and latrines advertise territories.

Breeding in temperate Europe usually lasts from spring into early autumn, with a shorter season in colder regions. Gestation is about three weeks; litters commonly contain four to six pups, and females may produce several. Newborns are hairless and blind, sheltered in a grass nest; their eyes open within days. They are weaned at two to three weeks, leave the nest soon after, and may mature in their first year.

By burrowing, feeding and moving through wetlands, the vole helps create conditions that other plants and animals can use. Burrowing and droppings alter soil structure and nutrient cycling. It is prey for native predators and, in Britain, introduced American mink. Dispersing juveniles can recolonize empty patches, linking local populations across wetlands.

The IUCN’s 2023 Least Concern assessment reflects the species’ broad range and mostly stable global trend, while recognizing regional declines. In Britain it is Endangered in England and Great Britain, and Near Threatened in Scotland. Agricultural intensification, pollution and watercourse development have destroyed and fragmented British water vole habitat. Introduced American mink can enter burrows and intensify predation; river restoration and mink control are part of recovery work.
